vignette: Three years ago, during the occupation that forced her family into hiding, Valeria watched armored patrols sweep through her neighborhood with absolute impunity. Soldiers systematically confiscated food and medical supplies, and when a security cordon cornered her in a stairwell, heavy hands pinned her shoulders to the wall, holding her completely still until the threat passed. The arbitrariness of the violence and the inescapable loss of physical autonomy left her fundamentally unmoored. Now a forty-four-year-old Latin American diplomat working out of a secure embassy wing in Washington, she had come to believe that chaos governed all human institutions. During a morning security briefing, a colonel detailed troop rotations and armored convoy routes along volatile borders. As military topics unfolded on the projected maps, the familiar cold dread pooled in her stomach. The detailed accounts of force deployment immediately stripped away any sense that her diplomatic work held lasting value, convincing her that nothing in her life felt meaningful anymore in the face of such overwhelming power. That hollow conviction of lost meaning triggered a frantic internal scramble. Valeria would retreat to her office, determined not to think about the briefing, forcing her mind toward neutral spreadsheets. Yet the suppression only created a vacuum; she found herself circling the same questions, going over and over why the event happened to her specifically, convinced that tracing the pattern of her suffering would finally provide answers. This relentless meaning-seeking quickly fractured her professional judgment. She began second-guessing every policy recommendation, certain she couldn’t trust that she would do the right thing. When embassy staff engaged in blatant misbehavior over resource allocation, Valeria interpreted their actions as a familiar moral violation. The sight of colleagues prioritizing office politics over ethical duty deepened her dehumanization, leaving her feeling like an object, not like a person. In response to this mounting certainty, she leaned heavily on suppression again, trying hard not to think about the trauma when it flared. But the constant mental bracing kept her hypervigilant, so the sudden, confining press of bodies in a crowded elevator felt exactly like those heavy hands pinning her to the wall. The feeling of being physically restrained immediately flooded her with self-doubt, confirming her fear that she was fundamentally incapable of navigating her new life safely, which drove her to circle the same questions again. Over months, these habits accumulated quietly but destructively. Valeria stopped attending interagency coordination meetings, citing scheduling conflicts, when in truth she could not bear the risk of hearing about troop movements or witnessing staff compromises. Her solitary routine grew narrower than any single relationship. She finally sought help after a routine diplomatic reception, where a guest’s animated story about border security sent her retreating to a supply closet, her hands shaking as she tried to suppress the memories while her mind spiraled into why she survived. What frightened her most was not the memories themselves, but the quiet certainty that she would never feel real in her own life again, and what she was most hoping for was a way to reclaim her voice without being crushed by the past.
